title: When one chip is not enough
kicker: 20 · When one chip is not enough

scenes.name: the capacity wall and the 405b model
scenes.visual: A physical memory capacity diagram comparing frontier model weights to single-chip capacities. Llama 3 405B at 16-bit takes 810 gigabytes. Against an 80 gigabyte H100, the model requires 11 GPUs. A DGX chassis of 8 GPUs holds 640 gigabytes, forcing the model to spill across two boxes.

beats.say: Even if memory bandwidth were infinite, frontier models hit a hard wall before running a single calculation: capacity.
beats.show: A capacity comparison bar shows frontier weights in hundreds of gigabytes versus single-chip capacities.

beats.say: An H one hundred holds eighty gigabytes, and an H two hundred holds one hundred and forty-one gigabytes. No amount of bandwidth helps if the model cannot physically fit.
beats.show: Memory capacity chips display: 'H100: 80 GB', 'H200: 141 GB'.

beats.say: At sixteen bits, Llama three four hundred and five billion takes eight hundred and ten gigabytes of weights alone, requiring eleven H one hundreds before allocating a single byte for working memory.
beats.show: Weight calculation displays: '405 billion × 2 bytes = 810 GB (needs 11 × 80 GB GPUs)'.

beats.say: A standard chassis of eight H one hundreds holds six hundred and forty gigabytes. At sixteen bits, the weights spill into a second chassis, forcing communication out onto the cluster network.
beats.show: Two DGX boxes appear: Box 1 (640 GB, full) and Box 2 (170 GB spillover). Takeaway: 'models exceeding 640 GB must span multiple chassis and cross external network links'.

scenes.name: what an interconnect link is
scenes.visual: A physical link schematic between two GPUs. Wires run across circuit boards and connectors. Emphasizes that link bandwidth obeys the exact same width-times-frequency law as on-chip buses, but across longer physical distances.

beats.say: When a model is split across chips, they must communicate continuously. What joins them is an interconnect link.
beats.show: A diagram joins GPU A to GPU B via physical copper link lanes.

beats.say: An interconnect link is simply a bundle of wires between chips, governed by the exact same width times frequency arithmetic as any internal bus.
beats.show: Bus formula highlights: 'bandwidth = wire count × bit rate per wire ÷ 8'.

beats.say: The only difference is distance. Fewer wires stretching across longer physical space mean slower speeds and higher energy per bit.
beats.show: Physical comparison: thousands of micrometre-short wires on-package versus dozens of centimetre-long wires on board.

beats.say: A chip has three distinct bandwidths: to its own memory, to a neighbouring chip, and out to the network. Each is several times slower than the last.
beats.show: Three tiers highlight: 'Local HBM', 'Neighbour NVLink', 'Network InfiniBand'. Takeaway: 'a GPU communicates across three tiers, each significantly slower than the last'.

scenes.name: scale-up versus scale-out
scenes.visual: Two architectural paradigms side by side. Scale-up: GPUs within a single box or rack linked via high-speed NVLink switches. Scale-out: separate server enclosures communicating across standard data-centre networking.

beats.say: Clustering divides cleanly into two domains: scale up and scale out.
beats.show: Split screen introduces 'Scale-up (inside the box)' on the left and 'Scale-out (between boxes)' on the right.

beats.say: Scale up connects graphics processors inside a single enclosure using high-speed proprietary links and crossbar switches.
beats.show: Scale-up box illuminates 8 GPUs joined by an internal NVSwitch crossbar fabric.

beats.say: Scale out connects separate chassis across the room through conventional data-centre network cables.
beats.show: Scale-out diagram connects chassis A to chassis B via rack switches and cables.

beats.say: The boundary between the two is the most critical line in a data centre: whatever data crosses that boundary pays a nine-fold penalty in speed.
beats.show: A bright dividing boundary highlights: 'Crossing the chassis boundary drops bandwidth by 9×'. Takeaway: 'the scale-up versus scale-out boundary is the defining bottleneck of distributed AI'.

scenes.name: why crossbar switches beat pairwise meshes
scenes.visual: Network topology comparison for eight GPUs. Left: Pairwise direct wiring requires 28 links, dividing each GPU's link budget seven ways. Right: A central switch where every GPU connects with full bandwidth, scaling linearly rather than quadratically.

beats.say: Wiring every pair of graphics processors directly together quickly becomes impossible as clusters grow.
beats.show: A direct pairwise mesh connects eight GPUs with a dense tangle of 28 links.

beats.say: Connecting every pair of n chips requires n times n minus one divided by two links: six links for four chips, twenty-eight for eight, and over two thousand five hundred for seventy-two chips.
beats.show: Pairwise scaling formula appears: 'Links = n(n - 1) / 2: 6 for 4 GPUs, 28 for 8, 2,556 for 72'.

beats.say: Because an H one hundred has a fixed budget of eighteen links, direct wiring splits each chip's bandwidth seven ways, leaving most links idle during point-to-point transfers.
beats.show: An H100 with 18 links splits them 7 ways: ~2.5 links per peer.

beats.say: A crossbar switch solves this completely. Every chip runs all its links straight to the switch, enabling any pair to communicate at maximum speed while connections scale linearly.
beats.show: A star topology converges onto central NVSwitch chips: every GPU enjoys full bandwidth. Takeaway: 'crossbar switches provide full-speed all-to-all communication without combinatorial wiring'.

scenes.name: the generational interconnect gap
scenes.visual: A generational timeline comparing local HBM bandwidth against bidirectional NVLink bandwidth across A100, H100, and B200. Local memory remains roughly seven to nine times faster than neighbour chip communication.

beats.say: Interconnect bandwidth has grown rapidly across generations, yet the ratio to local memory remains stubbornly fixed.
beats.show: A timeline displays: A100 (2020), H100 (2022), and B200 (2024).

beats.say: On the A one hundred, local memory ran at two terabytes per second while neighbouring links provided three hundred gigabytes per second each way, a gap of nearly seven times.
beats.show: A100 bar comparison: 'HBM 2,039 GB/s vs NVLink 300 GB/s each way (6.8× gap)'.

beats.say: On the H one hundred, memory grew to over three point three terabytes while links rose to four hundred and fifty gigabytes each way, maintaining a seven-point-four-fold gap.
beats.show: H100 bar comparison: 'HBM 3,352 GB/s vs NVLink 450 GB/s each way (7.4× gap)'.

beats.say: Blackwell reaches eight terabytes per second of memory and nine hundred gigabytes of link bandwidth each way. Local memory is always roughly eight times faster than reaching across the board.
beats.show: B200 bar comparison: 'HBM 8,000 GB/s vs NVLink 900 GB/s each way (8.9× gap)'. Takeaway: 'local memory remains roughly 7 to 9 times faster than peer GPU communication across all generations'.

scenes.name: geometry and the three bandwidth tiers
scenes.visual: A physical breakdown of the three bandwidth tiers. On package: 5,120 wires delivering 3,352 GB/s. Off package: 72 wire pairs delivering 450 GB/s each way (7.4x drop). Across the room: InfiniBand optical cable delivering 50 GB/s each way (9x drop again).

beats.say: Why is leaving the package so punishing? The answer is pure geometry.
beats.show: Physical diagram zooms from micro-bumps on silicon substrate out to optical transceiver cables.

beats.say: Inside the package, silicon interposers pack five thousand one hundred and twenty microscopic wires running over mere millimetres, delivering three point three five terabytes per second.
beats.show: Tier 1: 'HBM on-package · 5,120 wires · 3,352 GB/s'.

beats.say: Off the package, circuit boards accommodate only seventy-two wire pairs over centimetres, dropping bandwidth to four hundred and fifty gigabytes per second each way, over seven times slower.
beats.show: Tier 2: 'NVLink off-package · 72 wire pairs · 450 GB/s each way (7.4× drop)'.

beats.say: Across the room, an InfiniBand cable provides fifty gigabytes per second each way, nine times slower again. Driving longer distances demands vastly more power, forcing fewer wires and lower throughput.
beats.show: Tier 3: 'InfiniBand network · 1 cable · 50 GB/s each way (9× drop again)'. Takeaway: 'distance dictates bandwidth: package to board drops 7×; board to cable drops 9×'.

scenes.name: tensor parallelism and the all-reduce burden
scenes.visual: A worked example of tensor parallelism splitting an 8-term dot product across two GPUs. GPU A calculates 10, GPU B calculates 8. They exchange partial sums across the link so both finish with 18. An 80-layer model requires 160 all-reduces for every single generated token.

beats.say: Tensor parallelism splits the weight matrices of each layer across multiple graphics processors.
beats.show: A weight matrix and input vector split horizontally across GPU A and GPU B.

beats.say: To compute an output dot product, each chip multiplies its half of the inputs and weights, producing a partial sum.
beats.show: Calculations execute: 'GPU A produces partial sum 10', 'GPU B produces partial sum 8'.

beats.say: Before the next layer can begin, the chips must exchange their partial sums in an operation called an all-reduce, so both arrive at the complete answer of eighteen.
beats.show: Link exchange animates: partial sums swap across the link, summing to 18 on both GPUs.

beats.say: Modern architectures perform two all-reduces per layer. In an eighty-layer model, that means one hundred and sixty synchronization barriers for every single token generated. Inside a switch fabric that exchange is viable; across a network cable it is catastrophic.
beats.show: Token multiplication: '2 all-reduces/layer × 80 layers = 160 all-reduces per token'. Takeaway: '160 all-reduces per token make tensor parallelism viable only inside fast scale-up fabrics'.

scenes.name: expanding the fast domain
scenes.visual: Architectural evolution of the fast domain. DGX systems placed 8 GPUs in one NVLink domain. The GB200 NVL72 liquid-cooled rack integrates all 72 GPUs into a single massive NVLink domain holding 13.4 terabytes of memory.

beats.say: Because crossing between scale up and scale out is so punishing, the primary hardware strategy is to make the fast domain as large as possible.
beats.show: Strategy summary card: 'Rather than speeding up the network, expand the fast domain'.

beats.say: For years, the standard domain size was fixed at eight graphics processors in a single server chassis.
beats.show: Traditional 8-GPU chassis domain is highlighted.

beats.say: The liquid-cooled rack unites seventy-two graphics processors into a single seamless switch domain, containing over thirteen terabytes of memory.
beats.show: The GB200 NVL72 rack illuminates: 72 GPUs and 13.4 TB memory unified by NVLink switches.

beats.say: Any chip in the entire rack can reach any other at full link bandwidth, keeping even massive frontier models inside the fast neighbourhood and off the external network.
beats.show: Rack crossbar highlights full 1.8 TB/s peer bandwidth. Takeaway: 'rack-scale switch domains keep frontier models entirely within the fast neighbourhood'.

checks.claim: Llama 3 405B weights at 16-bit: 405e9 * 2 bytes = 810 GB, requiring 11 H100s (80 GB each)
DGX chassis capacity: 8 * 80 = 640 GB, spillover = 810 - 640 = 170 GB
Interconnect bandwidth ratios per direction: HBM 3,352 to NVLink 450 is 7.4x; NVLink 450 to InfiniBand 50 is 9.0x
All-reduces per token: 2 per layer * 80 layers = 160
